newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Germans feel the force of the occult.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Germans feel the force of the occult.

text.p: Under cover of darkness, black-clad figures slipped quietly between the tombstones of a Cologne cemetery before coming to a halt outside the mortuary.

The mysterious intruders broke in, removed a coffin containing a woman's body and dragged it outside. They lit candles and held a black mass which culminated in the mutilation of the body with knives until it was no longer recognisable.
The case made lurid headlines in Germany's mass market newspapers late last year, serving as a timely reminder that interest in the occult is alive and well in the 1990s.
While today's occultism may have its roots in beliefs dating back centuries, it also contains elements which are right up to date -- such as the Internet and links to neo-Nazi groups.

Many experts report an upsurge in interest in the occult as modern society leaves people feeling isolated and searching for a sense of belonging. Youngsters going through puberty are particularly vulnerable.

"Over the last 10 years, I think there's been a consistent rise in interest in this sort of thing," said Wolfgang Hund, the author of several books on the occult who holds seminars to warn young people of the dangers of flirting with the supernatural.

"It's to do with the disillusionment in society in general and the helplessness many young people now feel," said Joachim Keden, who forms part of a network of pastors appointed by the Protestant church across Germany to monitor cults and sects.

"The interest in the occult is connected to changes in traditional values," added Ulrich Paschold, an official in the Ministry for Family and Youth Affairs who monitors the activities of sects and occult groups.
NEO-NAZI LINKS
Keden says the problem exists throughout the western world, where the increasing emphasis on the individual has left many feeling unable to cope, but Germany has its own peculiarities.
"What we in Germany have registered is an increase in vandalism with religious connotations," he said.

The Cologne case is one high-profile example and Keden says the desecration of gravestones, the daubing of satanic symbols such as the star-shaped pentagram on church walls, and even arson attacks on churches have also become more common.
Germany's occult groups, like many of their counterparts in Scandinavia and northern Europe, also tend to have links with the right-wing extremist scene.
Not only do the two movements offer a feeling of belonging and a sense of order, they share a common interest in old Germanic history and ancient Norse gods.
"If you go into a shop specialising in esoteric stuff, you'll see books on runes and on old Germanic gods," Hund said. "There's certainly a connection between the occult and the neo-Nazi scene."

Like enthusiasts of everything from phonecards to football, occultists are also present on the Internet, spreading information about their practices and advertising products such as ouija boards, books and other accessories.

"Genuine magic mirror!" one purveyor of paranormal paraphernalia advertises. "This mirror is the ideal instrument for getting in contact with religious leaders and enabling astral journeys...385 marks ($240)."
But German organisations warning of the dangers of dabbling with the nether world are also in cyberspace.

"Around two thirds of adolescents have come into active or passive contact with occult practices," says the page of the Society for Scientific Examination of Parasciences -- a self-styled "consumer protection agency" for the occult.
"Many have not experienced a religious upbringing, they are like illiterates in the language of religion."
No one can put an exact figure on the number of Germans who are involved in the occult, precisely because the movement is secretive by its very nature.
Even trying to pin down which areas are hotbeds of occultism or the gender of most participants is difficult.
"When it gets to really hardcore things, then there are more men because it's all about power. But women are involved too as the sexual element also plays a big role," Hund said.
DEADLY GAMES
Hund, who uses magic tricks to demonstrate there is nothing supernatural about many of the practices in the occult, says even the most trivial dabblings can have fatal consequences.

In his local area, close to Nuremberg, a few years ago, five youths held a seance to summon up the spirit of a dead friend. The "spirit" told them they would die the same year. Two of the group committed suicide before the year was out.

Hund blames the media, and teenage magazines in particular, for trivialising the issue. "They irresponsibly celebrate the occult again and again. They give out instruction manuals for black masses," he charged.
Experts agree the best way to protect young people from the dangers of the occult is to educate them and their families.
"It's important not to leave them in their isolation," Keden said. "The state also has a responsibility, not just to educate and inform in this area but also to give young people new hope."
Government officials point out the state does not just have the power to educate and inform -- it can also clamp down hard if occult groups are violating the law.

The experts are unsure how interest in the occult will develop in the future, but Hund fears the approach of the new millennium will bring with it new feelings of insecurity and uncertainty which could play into the hands of the occultists.
"If you look at what was happening in Europe at the turn of the last millennium, it was hysteria," he said.
